title: Memorial of the Presentation of the Virgin Mary
meditation: Some Sadducees, those who deny that there is a resurrection, came forward and put this question to Jesus, saying, “Teacher, Moses wrote for us, If someone’s brother dies leaving a wife but no child, his brother must take the wife and raise up descendants for his brother. ” Luke 20:27–29

In today’s Gospel, it is the Sadducees’ turn to take their shot at trapping Jesus. The Sadducees were a priestly, aristocratic sect closely tied to Temple worship and political collaboration with Rome. In contrast with the Pharisees, they denied the resurrection of the dead, the immortality of the soul, and the existence of angels—all of which were foundational to Jesus’ own teachings. They accepted only the Torah, the first five books of Moses, as authoritative, which is why they crafted their hypothetical question from Mosaic Law.

They presented a scenario in which seven brothers successively marry the same woman, each dying without leaving children. After the woman also dies, they ask whose wife she will be at the resurrection. Their hypothetical was not intended to discover truth but to ridicule the idea of resurrection itself. However, Jesus calmly meets their skepticism with divine insight. He reveals that life in the resurrection is not a mere extension of the earthly existence we enjoy today. In the age to come, marriage as we know it will no longer exist because the faithful will share in a glorified existence that is immortal, spiritual, and wholly united to God.

Jesus then turns the Torah against them and points to God’s words from the burning bush: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Jesus explains that God “is” the God of their forefathers not “was.” This insight revealed the immortality of the soul, since God Himself spoke in the present tense.

This exchange showcases Jesus’ unmatched wisdom and desire to lead His opponents to the truth by revealing eternal realities with clarity. His teachings were so insightful that some scribes who believed in the resurrection replied, “Teacher, You have answered well.” Perhaps some of them were won over by divine wisdom.

Imagine sitting down with Jesus and asking Him anything. What would you ask? Perhaps there is something in your life that you do not understand—why God permitted a certain suffering or trial, for example. Or perhaps you have more general questions, such as how certain scientific theories can coexist with divine revelation when they appear to be in conflict. Deep down, many people believe in God and the faith He revealed, but lack clarity, especially regarding difficult topics. Though this may lead some to doubt, it leads others to a holy curiosity that seeks not to trap God, but to humbly seek His divine wisdom and knowledge.

Reflect today on any questions you may have about God, suffering, or the meaning of events in your life. Jesus holds every perfect answer to every question we could ask. In the light of His Truth, all things make sense. Hold onto that faith and hope, and seek out the truth you need to resolve any confusion in your heart. God desires to speak to you, grant you understanding, and affirm with clarity and conviction every truth you now hold in faith.

Lord of all Truth, at times I struggle with confusion, and that confusion can lead to doubt. Please grant me the gift of a pure and unwavering faith, especially when I encounter mysteries that are difficult to understand. When I am burdened by questions or uncertainty, dear Lord, grant me the gifts of wisdom, knowledge, and understanding. Help me to deepen my faith, to cling to Your Word, and to confidently proclaim Your truth to others. Jesus, I trust in You.

title: Friday of the Thirty-third Week in Ordinary Time
meditation: Today’s Gospel opens what is arguably the most dramatic and consequential week in human history. Jesus arrives in Jerusalem for the weeklong Feast of Passover, welcomed with jubilation by the crowds who had become His disciples over the previous three years of public ministry. The city is alive with expectation. Many wonder if this is the moment He will assert His Kingship and restore the United Kingdom of Israel. However, on the first day of the feast, Jesus takes a startling action: He enters the Temple and drives out the merchants, rebuking them for turning His Father’s house into a “den of thieves.”

Passover was the most sacred feast on the Jewish calendar, commemorating Israel’s deliverance from slavery in Egypt. It recalled the night the angel of death passed over the homes marked by the blood of a sacrificed lamb, which began the forty-year journey through the desert into the Promised Land.

Centuries later, King Solomon built the Temple on Mount Moriah, the very place where Abraham was tested in his willingness to sacrifice Isaac—a prefiguration of the sacrifice made by God the Father of His only Son on that same mount in Jerusalem. Since then, Jews from every tribe made an annual pilgrimage there to worship, recall God’s covenant with Abraham, and celebrate the Exodus.

During Passover, each family was required to offer an animal sacrifice at the Temple. To facilitate this, merchants sold lambs, goats, and doves, especially to pilgrims who had traveled long distances. Over time, however, what began as a practical service became deeply corrupted. Greed and commercialism replaced reverence. The sacred was eclipsed by profit.

Jesus’ cleansing of the Temple was a prophetic judgment. He was declaring that true worship must be restored. The Lamb of God had come to offer the definitive sacrifice, and the Temple would soon give way to a new and eternal covenant centered on Christ’s own Body, to be sacrificed and His flesh consumed.

This context helps us understand why the chief priests, scribes, and leaders of the people sought to put Jesus to death. He was disrupting a system they had long maintained—one that had become increasingly entangled with pride, financial gain, and empty ritual. From the pilgrimage and sacrifices to the flow of money that supported the Temple and, in some cases, enriched its leaders, much was at stake.

One important lesson we can draw from this clash is that when we stray from our central duty of divine worship and begin to elevate man-made customs over the purity of worship itself, we too are in need of a cleansing from the Lord. While human traditions can be deeply meaningful, they become a spiritual obstacle when treated as an end rather than a means to holiness.

For example, we may cling to devotional practices, liturgical preferences, or parish customs that once deepened our faith, but over time may have become routine, prideful, or divisive. When the form overshadows the substance, or personal preference outweighs reverence, humility, and obedience, even good traditions can hinder true worship.

Reflect today on the central mission of your life: divine worship. This is what you were made for and the means by which you become a member of God’s Kingdom. Though religious devotions and preferences can be helpful, consider whether your religious customs, habits, or personal opinions cloud the purity of your worship. Are you more concerned about the externals and customs, or worshiping God? If it is the former, ask the Lord to overturn those distortions and call you, your parish, and His entire Church back to sacred worship.

Most holy Lamb of God, as You entered the Temple during Passover and beheld the distortions that had crept into that sacred feast, Your holy zeal moved You to cleanse the Temple. Please cleanse the temple of my soul with that same divine zeal. Purge me of all superficial religious attachments and preferences, that I may be truly free to worship You in spirit and in truth. Jesus, I trust in You.

title: Thursday of the Thirty-third Week in Ordinary Time
meditation: Dear brothers and sisters in Christ,

As Jesus drew near Jerusalem, he saw the city and wept over it, saying, “If this day you only knew what makes for peace—but now it is hidden from your eyes. For the days are coming upon you when your enemies will raise a palisade against you; they will encircle you and hem you in on all sides.” Luke 19:41–43

Those with the gift of empathy are moved when they witness another person filled with sorrow to the point of weeping. Today’s Gospel invites us to gaze upon our Lord’s holy sorrow and weep with Him as He enters Jerusalem during the week of Passover when He would suffer and die. We continue to weep with His sorrowful Heart even now, as He gazes upon us and our world.

Sorrow is a natural and morally neutral emotion. We may grieve over many things: giving our all in a losing athletic contest, receiving a devastating health diagnosis, or losing a loved one in a tragic accident. All of these instances are natural and understandable.

However, we can also grieve for selfish reasons. We may grieve because our pride has been wounded or because we have been denied a worldly comfort, recognition, or success we desired. Such sorrow, rooted in self-love, does not elevate the soul and can lead to self-pity or resentment. In contrast, the sorrow of Christ is pure, selfless, and redemptive. He does not weep for Himself; He weeps for us—for souls who reject the grace of conversion, for hearts hardened against truth, and for a world that so often turns away from the very source of peace.

In Jesus’ lament over Jerusalem, we witness the sorrow of a God who deeply loves His people and desires their salvation, yet respects their freedom, even when that freedom is misused. His tears are a profound expression of divine empathy, which is the grief of Love rejected. And just as He once wept over the holy city that failed to recognize the time of its visitation by the Messiah, so too does He grieve today when we close our hearts to His presence and remain blind to the path that leads to true peace.

How should we respond to Jesus’ Sorrowful Heart? One temptation is to ignore it, downplay it, or pretend that His sorrow is unimportant or irrelevant. Another temptation is to acknowledge His sorrow over our sins and those of the world but then react with defensiveness, guilt, or discouragement. The holy response is to feel empathy for, and with, our Lord—to gaze upon His holy sorrow and the causes of that sorrow.

To look honestly and empathetically at our sins, the sins of the world, and the effect they have on the Sacred Heart of Jesus, is itself an act of charity. By doing so, we participate in the charity of Christ. He does not grieve out of anger, self-pity, or condemnation; He grieves out of love for every sinner. That love stirs the human emotion of compassion in His Sacred Humanity and expresses the infinite charity of His Divine Nature. His grief becomes a channel of grace that when properly understood and embraced, opens our hearts to that grace and compels us to conversion, both in our own lives and in the lives of those around us.

Reflect today on the sorrow in the Heart of Christ as He looks upon your life, your community, the Church, and the world. Allow yourself to sit with Him in that sorrow, not in despair or fear, but in love and solidarity. Let His grief move your heart with compassion. Ask yourself what causes Him sorrow in your own life. Is it a sin you cling to? A refusal to forgive? A hardness of heart, indifference to grace, or neglect of prayer? Let that holy sorrow move you to repentance, intercession, acts of love, and a deeper commitment to living for Him. In doing so, you will console the Heart of Christ and join in His redemptive mission, helping to bring peace to a world so in need of His grace.

My sorrowful Lord, as You gazed upon Jerusalem, Your Sacred Heart was pierced with grief. You saw clearly the suffering that would come upon Your people because they refused to turn to You. I know You look upon my heart with that same love and longing. Please give me the grace to see what You see, to feel what You feel, and to respond with a heart open to Your mercy. May my empathy for Your sorrow lead me to greater faith, deeper love, and a more complete union with You. Jesus, I trust in You.

title: Dedication of the Basilicas of Saints Peter and Paul, Apostles
meditation: The parable Jesus tells today reflects this divine reality. The nobleman who travels to a distant country to receive a kingship and later returns symbolizes Jesus Himself, who would soon depart this world through His Passion and Ascension, only to return in visible and permanent glory. The servants who are entrusted with coins represent all of us who are called to live by faith during His apparent absence. They are expected to invest, multiply, and bear fruit with what they have received, not sit idle in fear or spiritual complacency.

Jesus, knowing what lay ahead, sought to correct the false assumptions of the crowd. His Kingdom would not come with spectacle or worldly power. It would begin humbly, like a seed hidden in the soil. And it would grow through the fidelity of those who believe, invest their gifts, and remain vigilant for His return.

title: Memorial of Saint Elizabeth of Hungary, Religious
meditation: As we honor this saintly noblewoman, ponder her choice to follow Christ in the midst of so many temptations and trials. As you do, follow her example by making the will of God the greatest treasure of your life.

Two years before, a large entourage and dowry from her father had accompanied Elizabeth to the court of the Landgrave of Thuringia. There, she received a Catholic upbringing, an excellent education, and was cared for by attendants (ladies-in-waiting). She learned culture, manners, and royal protocol; attended banquets; wore fine clothing; and witnessed the intrigue and power struggles common in the royal court. The Castle of Wartburg in which she lived was a magnificent castle, and the Landgrave of Thuringia one of the richest in the empire. Life was extravagant, with poets and musicians, fine meals and social gatherings, and the best of what the world at that time had to offer. Behind the scenes, many factions plotted and formed alliances, seeking power and favors. Despite the challenges and worldly temptations she was thrust into at such a young age, Elizabeth grew in faith. She prayed, practiced mortification, and fell deeply in love with her Lord.

During the first ten years in Wartburg Castle, Elizabeth and her future husband, Louis IV, were raised together and formed a deep personal and spiritual bond. Though the marriage was arranged, they put their minds, hearts, and wills into what would soon become their future together. Louis’ father died when he was sixteen years old, and Louis became the Landgrave of Thuringia. Four years later, Elizabeth and Louis were wed.

From the very beginning, Elizabeth did not fit in with the courtly life. She was sensitive to the poor, sought virtue, and preferred simplicity, which made her an object of gossip and slander among the more “refined” members of the court. In Louis, however, she found a strong support. He admired her virtues and goodness and dismissed any criticism that came to his ears, defending her before all.

About two years after their marriage, when Elizabeth was sixteen, Franciscan friars arrived at the castle to care for the spiritual needs of the royal court. The holy Friar Conrad of Marburg became Elizabeth’s spiritual director. Through him, she learned about the saintly life of Saint Francis who probed the highest heights of holiness, even being pierced with the stigmata at the end of his life by a Seraphim, the highest of the choirs of angels, earning him the revered title “the Seraphic Father.” Stories of Saint Francis, the influence of the friars, and her own devotional life drew her deeper into the mysteries of faith. One story relates that one time, while praying in the castle chapel, she took off her royal crown, placed it before the Crucifix, and then lay prostrate before her Lord in prayer. When her mother-in-law saw this, she chastised Elizabeth, telling her such a gesture was beneath her dignity. Elizabeth responded, “How can I, a wretched creature, continue to wear a crown of earthly dignity, when I see my King Jesus Christ crowned with thorns?”

Elizabeth’s heart was inflamed with a desire for charity and justice. If she saw an injustice, she quickly sought to remedy it. Rather than eat food that was unjustly obtained, she preferred to go hungry. If the poor were cheated, she paid the debt owed them out of her own money. She loved to go down to the villagers, especially the poor, and bring them food, clothing, and whatever else they needed. She distributed these goods personally, in the company of her maids. This humility and generosity won her the love and respect of the peasant class, despite the ongoing ridicule of the nobility. When the nobility complained to her husband, he continued to support her and her charitable works.

One day, when Elizabeth was secretly bringing bread from the castle to the poor, she encountered her husband in the street. He had been told that she was stealing from the castle, so he asked her what she was carrying in her apron. When she opened it, beautiful roses appeared, to the delight of Louis who saw that as a sign of divine favor that humbled her detractors. On another occasion, she brought a leper into her own bedroom and laid him on her bed to care for him. Later, when Louis was told what Elizabeth did by her indignant mother-in-law, Louis went to strip the infected sheets from their shared bed. When he did so, he either saw in a vision, or was given an infused spiritual intuition that it was Christ Himself Whom Elizabeth cared for in the person of the leper. This only deepened Louis’ admiration for his young wife.

In 1227, at the age of twenty-six, Louis joined the army of Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II for the sixth crusade against the Muslims to take back the Holy Land which had been lost in 1187. On the way, disease spread through the troops and Louis fell ill, dying shortly afterwards. News of her husband’s death was devastating to the twenty-year-old Elizabeth. She and Louis had previously made vows to each other not to remarry if either of them died, so Elizabeth turned her eyes more fully to Chirst, devoting herself to His mission, no matter where He led.

Elizabeth and Louis had three children together. Their youngest, Gertrude, with whom Elizabeth was still pregnant when Louis died, grew up and became abbess of Altenburg Abbey. Their middle child, Sophie, married Henry II, Duke of Brabant. Their oldest, Hermann, initially succeeded his father as Landgrave of Thuringia when he was only four. Though Elizabeth acted on her son’s behalf in the governance of the Landgrave, Louis’ brother, Henry, seized control as regent for young Hermann and ran Elizabeth and her children out of the castle, causing many of the nobles to reject her. Hermann died unexpectedly several years later before he could make his claim as Landgrave, and Henry assumed full control.

Wandering for a while with two of her handmaids, Elizabeth entrusted her children to the care of some of Louis’ sympathetic family members. Eventually, the family members were able to secure Elizabeth refuge in the Castle of Marburg where, with the guidance of Friar Conrad, she fully dedicated herself to God’s service with private vows, took a gray habit, and formed a small community with other friends. Louis’ family secured for her the remainder of her dowry, which she used to build a hospital for the poor. She spent the next three years caring for the sick in the humblest of ways. In 1231, at the age of twenty-four, Elizabeth came down with a high fever and after days of suffering, offered herself to God. When the people heard of her illness, they flocked to her in prayer. Soon after her death, miracles were attributed to her intercession. People became so devoted to her that only four years after her death, Pope Gregoy IX canonized her and built a church in Marburg in her honor.

Saint Elizabeth of Hungary was given all the privileges and wealth this world had to offer her at a very young age, yet in her heart, none of that compared to the privilege of serving her Lord, especially as he was present to her in the sick and poor. She chose the better part and will forever rejoice with her God in Heaven.

As we honor this saintly noblewoman, ponder her choice to follow Christ in the midst of so many temptations and trials. As you do, follow her example by making the will of God the greatest treasure of your life.

title: Friday of the Thirty-second Week in Ordinary Time
meditation: Today as we are ending the liturgical year Jesus is emphasizing on the end of times. Indeed, he is reminding us that the Lord’s Day will come like a thief. Jesus is telling this because as it is remarkable people try to maximize their pleasure but then we are told to be aware because the end of our time will be on an unknown day and this end will be unique. Consequently, life with God matters more than everything we can think because all will be laid down but our soul will campaign us. In this sense, Saint John tells us to be aware of antichrist that fights the teachings which they have received, antichrist’s ideologies are having hidden faces. Meanwhile, there has been the movement of false prophet even today, that mislead people. It’s our task to ask ourselves if we are still remembering the promises we have made with God if we are not following the spirit of the World. We ask the Grace of being faithful until the last breath and the spirit of discernment

title: Memorial of Saint Josaphat, Bishop and Martyr
meditation: Beloved, today we are celebrating the martyrdom of Saint Josaphat, the testimony of faith. The readings that we are given lead us to three main points especially in the gospel, Jesus tells us to be aware of the day of the coming for none knows the day and hour. Nevertheless, waiting for this day there are some attitudes that are requested as we get it from address to Philemon to be a resilient person in the belief of change. The former thief and slave Onesm became a child because of acceptation of Jesus in his imprisonment. Otherwise, we all have a debt to pay as Paul reminded Philemon that we all live all by favor and reconcile with our fellows who are mistaken.

title: Memorial of Saint Martin of Tours, Bishop
meditation: Today we are reminded to essential conviction. The first one is that we live of divine Providence by the healing of the ten lepers in the Gospel all cried (Lk17,11-19) but one only recognized how wondrous was his life because of God’s mercy. Indeed, this recognition gives freedom of heart and is a source of many blessings; are you aware that you live of God’s favor? Are you thankful or are you always keen for blessing waited rather than enjoying the graces already given? Consequently if someone has that grateful heart he/she knows how to behave before leaders(Tt3,1-7). Today, we are asked to pray for leaders rather than insulting them. Remember to pray for peace especially for countries with troubles and pray that God may take over the Leaders and be their light.

title: Memorial of Saint Leo the Great, Pope and Doctor of the Church
meditation: Today we are celebrating the feast of Saint Leon the Great, the readings of today are calling us to bear a worthy moral conduct. We are meditating on the role of responsible of the community as we see Tithe as an example (Tt2:1-8.11-14) Paul is reminding him to be a good example not only in conduct but also in his teachings as he received those teachings from the apostles. Nevertheless, today we are reminded that we are the light in whatever category we can belong. We are the light or darkness of someone. Indeed, nowadays, the world exalts the maximization of pleasure through drinking and self-enjoyment; Saint Paul makes an alert on elderly and young to bear out an exemplary life that leads to salvation of others. Even Jesus stresses that attitude of being good servants without need of much appreciation but rather as a personal responsibility that we have to offer the world (Lk17,7-10). Ask yourself a question:” Am I worthy of trust?”

title: Feast of the Dedication of the Lateran Basilica in Rome
meditation: Today we are celebrating the dedication of the St John Lateran basilica; the readings of today are calling us to acknowledge the fact that we are true temples of God. Indeed, in the second reading(1Co3,9b-11.16-17) reminds us that we are the temple of God and that we have a greater chance to have a greatest  foundation who is Jesus Christ and to always meditate on that privilege. In the Gospel (Jn2, 13-22), Jesus shows us that He is unshaken even by the powers of death and hell can’t alter his Power and being. Therefore, he shows it by throwing unworthy acts that were being undertaken in the Temple. Indeed, God is jealous of our evil doing and if we forget that we are temple of God and we have Jesus as a foundation we are led to our own perdition. Today let’s ask the grace of recognizing the abundance we are imbued with and never disappoint God.

title: Saturday of the Thirty-first Week in Ordinary Time
meditation: Dear brothers and sisters in Christ,

Today, Saint Paul helps us discover the power of trusting in God. When a person truly places his trust in Christ, he discovers within himself a strength that goes beyond his own abilities. With Christ, we can face difficulties, overcome our weaknesses and accomplish great things. Our strength does not come merely from our talents or personal efforts, but above all from our union with the Lord. That is why we should never lose heart in the face of difficulties, because whoever walks with Christ is never abandoned.

However, one of the greatest victories we are called to achieve in life is the victory of self-control. We live in a world full of temptations, which sometimes take very ordinary forms: gluttony, the excessive pursuit of pleasure, lack of discipline, and dishonesty in the management of money. Jesus particularly warns us against the misuse of wealth and the danger of becoming slaves to money. Indeed, it is not enough to be capable of accomplishing great things; we must also learn to control our desires, remain honest in our actions and keep our hearts free from attachment to worldly possessions. The true greatness of a Christian is also revealed in the ability to resist evil, even when nobody is watching.

Dear brothers and sisters, let us ask the Lord to give us the strength to live with this inner freedom. May our trust in Christ help us overcome our weaknesses and prevent us from being dominated by our appetites, personal interests or the attraction of money. Let us learn to be faithful in little things, because it is often through the ordinary actions of our daily lives that the quality of our Christian life is revealed. Let us not seek only to accomplish great things with Christ; let us above all strive to remain faithful to him in the little things of everyday life.
Father Dieudonné MANIRAGUHA

title: Friday of the Thirty-first Week in Ordinary Time - Our Citizenship Is in Heaven
meditation: Dear brothers and sisters in Christ,

Saint Paul reminds us of a fundamental truth of our faith: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil 3:20). These words invite us never to lose sight of our true identity and our ultimate destination. Certainly, we live in this world, where we have responsibilities, projects and commitments, but we must never forget that our permanent home is with God. That is why we are called to live, even now, as citizens of heaven, allowing our choices, words and actions to be guided by the values of the Gospel. Preparing ourselves to enter our heavenly homeland means learning every day to love more deeply, to forgive, to serve others and to remain faithful to the Lord.

In today's Gospel (Lk 16:1-8), Jesus surprises us by praising the dishonest steward, not because of his dishonesty, but because of his resourcefulness and foresight. He knew how to take initiatives and use his intelligence to prepare for the future. In this way, Jesus invites us, too, to demonstrate creativity, discernment and determination in our spiritual journey. If people of this world are capable of using so much ingenuity to secure their earthly interests, how much more should the disciples of Christ put their intelligence, talents and resources at the service of God's Kingdom! Let us therefore not be passive in our faith. Rather, let us seek concrete ways of doing good, supporting others and making fruitful use of the gifts God has entrusted to us.

In this regard, the technological advances taking place in our world today, about which Pope Leo XIV invites us to reflect, particularly in his teaching on human dignity and technological progress, also offer us an opportunity to renew our Christian commitment. Technology is neither an end in itself nor a threat that must automatically be rejected; it can become a valuable instrument at the service of the Gospel, fraternity and human development, provided that it is used wisely and responsibly. Let us therefore put the possibilities of our time at the service of what is good, rather than allowing ourselves to become enslaved by them. The real question is not simply how far technological progress can take us in this world, but rather how we can use it to prepare ourselves better for our encounter with God. May all our initiatives, knowledge and talents help us draw closer to our heavenly homeland, where the Lord awaits us. Amen.
Father Dieudonné MANIRAGUHA

title: Thursday of the Thirty-first Week in Ordinary Time
meditation: Dear brothers and sisters in Christ, detachment and renunciation occupy an essential place in the life of every believer who desires to follow the Lord faithfully. Drawing from his own experience, Saint Paul invites us to consider the advantages and riches of this world as losses, even as rubbish, compared with the incomparable value of knowing Christ and living in communion with Him (Phil 3:7-8). Indeed, following Christ requires us to make choices, to renounce whatever separates us from God, and to recognize that nothing can compare with the joy of belonging to Him.

This detachment does not mean despising life or rejecting the gifts God has given us. Rather, it means having an inner freedom that prevents us from becoming slaves to worldly possessions and pleasures. It gives us the strength to resist sin, overcome our weaknesses and maintain a simple heart, always available and fully devoted to our Divine Master. Those who truly attach themselves to Christ gradually learn to detach themselves from everything that might take His place in their hearts.

Therefore, dear young people, both young and old, let us have the courage to put this Gospel teaching into practice. Let us learn to reject everything that is displeasing in the eyes of God and develop a genuine hatred for sin in all its forms. Let us not be carried away by passing pleasures or the temporary riches of this world. Instead, let us ask the Lord for a free and generous heart, ready to leave everything behind interiorly in order to follow Him more faithfully, for Christ Himself is the greatest treasure of our lives.
Father Dieudonné MANIRAGUHA

title: Memorial of Saint Charles Borromeo, Bishop
meditation: Dear brothers and sisters in Christ,

'Work out your salvation with fear and trembling,' Saint Paul exhorts us (Phil 2:12). Saint Augustine beautifully expresses this truth when he says: “God, who created us without us, will not save us without our cooperation.” These words remind us that salvation is first and foremost a free gift from God, but it also calls for our personal cooperation. God offers us His grace and invites us to respond through a life of faith, fidelity and commitment. We must therefore not remain passive, waiting for God to do everything for us, but rather allow ourselves to be transformed by His love and take our spiritual journey seriously.

That is why we must ask the Lord for the grace to work out our salvation each day through small acts of renunciation, as the Gospel invites us to do. Renouncing our pride, bad habits, disordered attachments and everything that separates us from God are concrete ways of showing our desire to follow Him. The journey towards salvation sometimes demands sacrifices, but no renunciation made out of love for God is ever in vain. May the Lord give us the courage not to be discouraged by the demands of the Gospel, but to follow Him faithfully each day, confident that His grace goes before us, accompanies us and ultimately leads us to eternal life.
Father Dieudonné MANIRAGUHA

title: Tuesday of the Thirty-First Week in Ordinary Time
meditation: Today, the Word of God invites us to remain ever open and ready to respond to God's call.

In our daily lives, it is all too easy to become caught up in numerous activities, some of which may seem indispensable, yet gradually lead us to overlook what is most essential: our life with God. This is often reflected in our relationship with Him, where our attachment to material possessions, money, and even family ties can sometimes become obstacles to our spiritual growth and Christian journey.

The twofold invitation in today's Gospel refers first to God's call to Israel and then to His invitation extended to all the nations. The Acts of the Apostles recounts this transition from Israel to the Gentiles, a decisive moment in the history of the Church, reminding us that God's salvation is intended for all humanity, without exception.

Dear brothers and sisters, the Lord invites us to walk with Him. He comes to meet us in great humility, as the first reading reminds us, so that He may become one of us and share in our human condition.
Let us therefore give Him our response and avoid every form of refusal. Indeed, the reasons that lead us to postpone or turn down God's invitations are not always beneficial to our lives.
May we never allow our earthly concerns to prevent us from welcoming the Lord into our hearts.
Wishing you all a blessed day!
Father Dieudonné MANIRAGUHA

title: Commemoration of all departed souls
meditation: My dear brothers and sisters,

On this day, when the Church raises her prayers to God for all the faithful departed, the Word of God invites us to turn our gaze towards Christ, the Lord of life, who calls all those who believe in him to share in the resurrection. Today's Gospel reminds us of a fundamental truth of our faith: we were not created for death, but for eternal life. God created us out of love and calls us to live forever in his presence. By giving himself to us as food in his Body and Blood, Christ has left us the pledge of this imperishable life: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him on the last day” (Jn 6:54).

The Solemnity of All Saints, which we celebrated yesterday, and today's Commemoration of All the Faithful Departed invite us to contemplate the profound mystery of the communion of the Church. Indeed, the Church is not limited to the community of believers who are still making their earthly pilgrimage. She also embraces those who, having completed their journey on earth, already enjoy the glory of heaven, as well as those who are still undergoing purification in preparation for the fullness of communion with God. This is what the Church's tradition describes as the three states of the one Church: the Church Triumphant, made up of the saints and the blessed who enjoy the glory of heaven; the Church Suffering, consisting of those who are still undergoing purification in the hope of entering fully into the presence of God; and the Church Militant, to which we still belong as we journey through this earthly life. These are three states of one and the same Church, united in Christ and destined to be gathered together in the fullness of the Kingdom of God.

In this perspective, the Commemoration of the Faithful Departed is not a celebration dominated by sadness or fear of death. Above all, it is a celebration of Christian hope. It invites us not to remain fixed on the tomb, but to raise our eyes towards the One who passed through death and conquered it once and for all: Jesus Christ, the firstborn from the dead (Col 1:18). With Saint Paul, we can therefore proclaim: “Death, where is your victory? Death, where is your sting?” (1 Cor 15:55). Death no longer has the final word, because the risen Christ has opened for us the way to eternal life. Through the sacraments, and especially through the Eucharist, he already communicates this new life to us and gives us the medicine of immortality, gradually drawing us into his own victory over death.

This is why we believe that our departed brothers and sisters have not been annihilated. Those who have left us in faith and hope have not fallen into nothingness; their lives remain in the hands of God. Death has not destroyed their existence; rather, it has marked their passage towards the encounter with the Lord to which we are all called. Although we do not know the particular path of purification of each soul, we know that God's mercy is infinitely greater than our human limitations. This is why the Church prays for her departed children, trusting in the power of divine mercy, which can lead them into the fullness of God's light.

All the acts of piety that we undertake on this day — our prayers, visits to cemeteries, acts of charity and, above all, the celebration of the Holy Eucharist — are therefore rooted in faith and love. We offer them for our departed brothers and sisters, asking the Lord, in his infinite goodness, to complete in them the work of purification and welcome them into the communion of saints. By praying for them, we also proclaim that the bonds of love are not broken by death and that our communion in Christ remains stronger than physical separation.

My dear brothers and sisters, on this day of remembrance, let us entrust all our departed loved ones to the loving tenderness of the Father. Let us pray for those whom we have loved, those whose memory we cherish, but also for all those who died in solitude, in obscurity, or without anyone to remember them in prayer. And as we intercede for them, let us renew our own hope: one day, we too shall cross the threshold of death and stand before the Lord. May this prospect encourage us to live now in faith, charity and fidelity to the Gospel.
Lord, grant eternal rest to all our departed brothers and sisters. May your perpetual light shine upon them, and may your mercy lead them into the joy of your Kingdom. May they rest in peace. Amen.
Father Dieudonné MANIRAGUHA

title: As he who called you is holy, be holy yourselves in all your conduct; for it is written: ‘You shall be holy, for I am holy.’” (1 Peter 1:15–16)- Solemnity of All Saints
meditation: Dear brothers and sisters in Christ, As we celebrate the Solemnity of All Saints today, allow me to begin this meditation with these words of exhortation from the Apostle Peter, who reminds us that holiness is the ultimate goal of the entire Christian life.

The saints whom we commemorate today were men and women of their own time. Like us, they experienced the joys and trials of human existence; like us, they believed in God and walked in faith. However, they left us a precious testimony through their lives, which remains a light and an encouragement on our journey towards God.

They form that vast and countless multitude presented to us in today's first reading. They now enjoy the fullness of happiness because they live in God's presence and are filled with His blessings. Indeed, the supreme joy of the saints consists in the beatific vision of God, in that eternal contemplation of the One who is the source of all love and happiness. Conversely, the greatest suffering of the damned consists precisely in being deprived forever of God's presence.

But we, dear brothers and sisters, are filled with firm hope: the hope that one day we shall behold the face of God and share in eternal happiness with all the saints who have gone before us. Saint John reminds us of this in the second reading: we are already children of God, although what we shall become has not yet been fully revealed. Nevertheless, we know that when Christ appears, we shall be like Him, because we shall see Him as He really is.

In the light of this hope, and in response to the invitation of the eight Beatitudes proclaimed in today's Gospel, Let us strive, dear brothers and sisters, to make the Gospel the true light of our lives. Holiness is not an ideal reserved for a few extraordinary people; it is a vocation addressed to each and every one of us. It is built day by day through our choices, our words, our attitudes and, above all, through the way we love God and our neighbour.

May our actions, therefore, reflect the charity of Christ, so that at the end of our earthly pilgrimage, the Lord may address these words of promise to us: “Come, you who are blessed by my Father; inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink; I was naked and you clothed me…” (Matthew 25:34–36).

May our patron saints intercede for us, accompany us through their prayers, and obtain for us the grace to follow Christ faithfully, until the day when we shall be united with them in the glory of the Kingdom of Heaven.
A blessed and holy Feast of All Saints to everyone!
